content: The following is a detailed explanation of the medical information provided: 1. Gastrointestinal Disorders: Patients may experience abdominal pain, discomfort, bloating, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. 2. General Disorders and Administration Site Conditions: Common symptoms include fatigue, a general feeling of being unwell, and malaise. 3. Metabolism and Nutrition Disorders: Fluid retention and weight gain have been reported. 4. Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue Disorders: Muscle spasms and pain in the extremities may occur. 5. Nervous System Disorders: Dizziness, headaches, and drowsiness (somnolence) are possible side effects. 6. Psychiatric Disorders: Sleep disturbances, such as insomnia, may develop. 7. Reproductive System and Breast Disorders: Symptoms can include breast pain, breast tenderness, and uterine bleeding. 8. Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue Disorders: Night sweats and itching (pruritus) are potential issues. 9. Vascular Disorders: Hot flashes and undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding are noted concerns. 10. Contraindications: Women with a history of breast cancer, known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia, active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), or arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke or myocardial infarction) should not use this therapy. Known hypersensitivity to estradiol, progesterone, or any excipients, as well as liver impairment or disease, protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other thrombophilic disorders, are contraindications. 11. Increased Risks with Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT): Estrogen plus progestin therapy is associated with an increased risk of PE, DVT, stroke, and myocardial infarction (MI). A slight increase in ovarian cancer risk was reported in the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin substudy. Women aged 65–79 years taking estrogen plus progestin or estrogen alone may have an increased risk of probable dementia. Postmenopausal women receiving estrogens have a 2to 4-fold increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery. 12. Hypercalcemia in Breast Cancer with Bone Metastases: Estrogen therapy may cause severe hypercalcemia in women with breast cancer and bone metastases. 13. Retinal Vascular Thrombosis: Women receiving estrogens may experience retinal vascular thrombosis. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if there is sudden partial or complete vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, or migraine. Permanent discontinuation is advised if papilledema or retinal vascular lesions are confirmed. 14. Endometrial Hyperplasia and Cancer: Adding progestin for at least 10 days of an estrogen administration cycle, or daily with continuous estrogen regimens, reduces the incidence of endometrial hyperplasia compared to estrogen alone. Endometrial hyperplasia may be a precursor to endometrial cancer. 15. 16. Hypertriglyceridemia and Pancreatitis: Women with preexisting hypertriglyceridemia may experience elevated plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis during estrogen therapy. 17. Breast Cancer Risk: Observational studies have reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller risk with estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use. Risks may persist for over 10 years after discontinuation. 18. Liver Function: Estrogens may be poorly metabolized in women with hepatic impairment. Caution is advised in women with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or pregnancy. Therapy should be discontinued if cholestatic jaundice recurs. 19. Thyroid Function: Estrogen administration increases thyroid-binding globulin levels. Women dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy may require an increased dose when receiving estrogens. 20. Fluid Retention: Estrogens and progestins can cause fluid retention. Caution is advised in women with conditions that may be affected, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction. Therapy should be discontinued if medically concerning fluid retention occurs. 21. Hypocalcemia in Hypoparathyroidism: Estrogen-induced hypocalcemia may occur in women with hypoparathyroidism. The risks and benefits of therapy should be carefully considered. 22. Residual Endometrial Implants: Women treated with estrogen-alone therapy post-hysterectomy may develop residual endometrial implants. Adding progesterone may be considered for these women. 23. Angioedema: Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of angioedema in women with hereditary angioedema. Risks and benefits should be evaluated. 24. Exacerbation of Preexisting Conditions: Estrogen therapy may worsen asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraines, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. Risks and benefits should be weighed in women with these conditions. 25. Serum FSH and Estradiol Levels: These levels have not been shown to be useful in managing moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms. 26. Stroke and Venous Thromboembolism (VTE): An increased risk of stroke and VTE has been demonstrated, particularly during the first year of therapy. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if a stroke or VTE occurs or is suspected. Estrogens should be discontinued 4–6 weeks before surgery associated with increased thromboembolism risk or during prolonged immobilization. 27. Breast Cancer Monitoring: Women should receive annual breast examinations by a healthcare provider, perform monthly breast self-examinations, and schedule mammography based on age, risk factors, and prior results. 28. Pregnancy and Lactation: Estrogens and progestins are not indicated for premenopausal, pregnant, or lactating women. Estrogens plus progestins are present in human milk and may reduce milk production. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the child. 29. Administration Instructions: Take the medication each evening with food. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible with food unless it is within 2 hours of the next dose. 30. Storage: Store the medication at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). This information is provided for general educational purposes and should be discussed with a healthcare provider for personalized guidance.
